probe_text: After round 8 the director wrote down its final label for each shape. Three probes then reused those labels in new instructions. Bare label → 6-round partner: the original matcher, which shares the full game history, resolves the labels almost perfectly (39/40). Negation: the same matcher picks "the one that is neither X nor Y" from a restricted 3-shape display — 20/20, so established labels immediately work as arguments of a logical operator they were never used with during the game. Bare label → fresh agent: an identical copy of the same model, seeing the same 8 shapes but none of the history, drops to 25/40. Same weights, same labels, same referents — the missing 36 points live entirely in the shared transcript.

discussion:
Symbols as interaction-bound constraints — supported. The strongest fact in the data is a controlled one: director and matcher are the same frozen network. Nothing that could count as a lexical convention exists in the weights of one agent and not the other. Yet the same label scores 98% inside the dyad that formed it and 62% outside it. Whatever the label's meaning-in-use is, it is stored in the shared transcript — the paper's "coordinative structure" — not in either network. That is the symbols-as-constraints picture (Rączaszek-Leonardi's, endorsed by the paper) in an unusually pure form, since the usual human confound (two different brains that might have internalized different things) is absent by construction.

"Ungrounding" — the paper's reformulated grounding challenge — partially observed. Rączaszek-Leonardi asks how forms become partly detached "from the ongoing stream of events so as to be amenable to rule-based manipulation." Operationalized here: once a dyad has settled on "the lightning bolt", can the token be used in constructions never seen in the game? Under negation — 20/20 — yes: the label functions as a manipulable argument, not a frozen stimulus-response routine. But detachment is only partial: transfer to an agent outside the interaction stays 36 points below within-dyad use. Detached enough for logic, still tethered to the history that made it. That intermediate status is exactly what the constraints-view predicts, and hard to square with a naive code-view in which a transparent description should work for everyone or no one.

Where LLM dyads diverge from humans: stability without economy. Human directors in Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs start near 20 words and compress round over round toward two-word conceptual pacts. These directors, told that words cost, started terse (~6 words), then lengthened on failure and froze whatever worked — consecutive-round lexical overlap reaches 1.0 (verbatim reuse) versus 0.10 for the no-history control, while mean length stays flat or rises. The convention-formation equilibrium is reached by form-freezing, not gradual streamlining. One reading: humans discover efficiency interactively because verbatim recall of their own past descriptions is costly, so re-referring compresses; an LLM re-reads its transcript for free, so the cheapest reliable move is exact repetition. The paper's claim that linguistic forms are "replicable constraints" whose utility lies in salient-affordance provision rather than form/content fidelity gets a twist here: for LLMs, fidelity itself is the affordance.

Audience design is inconsistent — a real deficit the paper points at. When the partner swap was announced, one director immediately re-expanded its formulas (and still missed until feedback), others kept 6-round-old shorthand with a partner who had never seen it. When the swap was covert, directors discovered it only through failure and repaired by elaboration. This is where the paper's Beer-derived critique — no continuous coupling, adaptation only inside the context window and only when the context makes the need legible — matches the data: adaptation happened, but it was reactive (feedback-driven) far more reliably than anticipatory (model-of-the-partner-driven).

What this does not test. The paper's deeper claims — process metaphysics, incrementality of split utterances, materially-grounded normativity — are untouched. This experiment operationalizes only the empirically tractable rim of the argument: conventions live in interaction histories, become manipulable tokens, and current systems adapt within, not across, encounters. A follow-up (Experiment B in the original sketch) would test whether a LoRA update distilled from the transcript turns a partner-specific convention into a partner-general disposition — the in-context vs in-weights boundary the paper treats as the static/dynamic divide.
limitations: Small scale: 7 games, 544 scored trials, one model (gemini-2.5-flash), one 8-item stimulus set. Curves are qualitatively consistent across dyads but per-condition means average over visible dyad heterogeneity.

One-shot protocol: the matcher cannot ask clarification questions, so the incremental repair dynamics the paper (via DS-TTR) treats as constitutive of dialogue are excluded by design; repair here happens only across trials via correct/wrong feedback.

The efficiency pressure is an instruction ("every word costs"), not an objective; it produced terse openings rather than human-like compression curves, which limits direct comparison with Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs.

Fresh-agent transparency (62%) partly reflects that honest visual descriptions of ASCII shapes are semi-transparent to any competent viewer; the theoretically meaningful quantity is the 36-point within-dyad advantage, not either number alone.
Negation probes used a restricted 3-shape display (chance 33%), so 20/20 shows label-under-operator competence, not full compositional generality.

Two instrument artifacts were caught and fixed mid-study (both documented in the repo): a strict answer parser that scored correct-but-misformatted choices as wrong (creating a false feedback death-spiral in one run-1 game), and a stale letter-display frame in delayed probes (deflating partner scores as clean permutations). Final data (run 3) is clean of both: zero audit flags, zero unparsed answers.
repro: Code, stimuli, per-trial JSON, full agent transcripts, and archived earlier runs (including both instrument bugs) at github.com/Cognitive-Modeller/llm-convention-games. Agents are gemini-2.5-flash on Vertex AI (temperature 0.7 director / 0.2 matcher, thinking budget 512/1024). Paradigm: Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs (1986) referential communication; partner-swap manipulation after Wilkes-Gibbs & Clark (1992); LLM adaptation baseline: Hawkins et al. (2020). Motivating paper: Gregoromichelaki & Mills (2025), Process and Dynamics in AI and Language Use, Topics in Cognitive Science. Total compute (measured): 61M input + 3.2M output tokens ≈ US$26 across all runs; the final clean run alone ≈ US$16. Wall-clock ≈ 2.5 h including the two re-runs.
